title: DSA: Exploiting the Carrion Party
author: Ari Paul
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Democratic_Socialists_of_America_jacket_from_San_Francisco_Bernie_Sanders_Rally_LA_Convention_Center_Los_Angeles_California_USA_49609093656-680x510.jpg)

Photograph Source: Cory Doctorow - [CC BY-SA
2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/)

The continued electoral success of the Democratic Socialists of America–whose
candidates run for Democratic Party nominations rather than as
independents–has a lot of people very angry. Most of these candidates when
judged by their policies are more FDR’s New Deal than worker-controlled
factories–a return to the party’s greatness rather than importing radical
politics into a centrist machine. But in the US that practically makes you a
Naxalite.

For mainstream Democrats this is a crisis. Challengers running on single-payer
health care, universal childcare and rent control are beating corporate
Democratic incumbents in party elections fair and square, and
[polling](https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/5952147-poll-democratic-
socialist-support/) shows that socialist ideas are indeed increasingly popular
in an unaffordable world. The party has evolved for decades away from the New
Deal and civil rights in pursuit of this moderate center accepted by socially
liberally rich donors who can live with gay marriage and abortion but need
their workplaces union-free. Now Bernie Sanders’ ideological grandkids are all
grown up, winning races and serving in office with the big D by their names,
co-opting this coveted brand status.

Some [pundits](https://www.wsj.com/opinion/socialists-lead-democrats-into-the-
tea-party-trap-c991b290) have likened this to the Tea Party candidates of
2010–right-wing populist insurgents who ousted old guard Republicans who were
seen as too entrenched in the sinecures and out-of-touch with the conservative
base. In other words, rather than start a new party in the November elections,
DSA, like the Tea Party, focused on the spring primaries–which are often the
real election in places where one major party dominates politics. This isn’t
just expediency–in both cases, DSA and Tea Party popularity have been fueled
by anti-incumbent angst.

Conservatives see this as a communist threat in the making. Once a critical
mass of DSA candidates get elected then socialists will have the ability to
steer one of the nation’s two major parties.

The DSA’s socialist critics see this choice to run inside the Democratic Party
as supreme disappointment. The entryist strategy means that elected DSA
members will have work within the confines of the Democrats, who are avowed
supporters of capitalism and American imperialism. Real socialists would run
independently, thus signalling to the working class that they are not going to
compromise with the class enemies who make up the Democratic Party donor base
and instead build a wholly separate and prefigurative structure.

All of these viewpoints about the DSA strategy to run candidates within the
Democratic Party misunderstand its contemporary nature. Once the organ of
FDR’s New Deal and LBJ’s Great Society, the Democrats’ weakness isn’t just
that theirs is a capitalist and imperialist party. The real problem: it’s not
a party at all.  
Major European political parties–for example, the British Labour Party, have
rules governing not just its candidates but its [member
base](https://labour.org.uk/resources/codes-of-conduct-and-welfare/) and a
policy manifesto that binds everyone together. Left critics of DSA’s electoral
strategy often say the moment one registers as a Democrat they have signed
their socialism away. But this action is simply checking a box on a card to
vote in a primary election–you don’t pay dues, answer to a local official or
abide by any code of conduct.

____As the scholar[Aziz Rana](https://www.bc.edu/bc-web/schools/law/academics-
faculty/faculty-directory/aziz-rana.html) [has pointed out](https://shout.lbo-
talk.org/lbo/RadioArchive/2025/25_04_24.mp3), the Democrats aren’t a party in
any real sense, but rather a network of operatives and consultants that
candidates can use as a fundraising vehicle for their own individual
campaigns. And so if a random businessman can do that to run a neoliberal
campaign on the Democratic line, why shouldn’t a socialist use the same tools?

These DSA electoral victories within the Democrats speak to the hollowness of
the current party–Democratic elders
[dismiss](https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/5938488-letitia-james-
mamdani-endorsements/) winners who offer universal programs on grounds that
they’re out of touch with the average voter, but the scoreboard says
otherwise. For the DSA’s left critics, the group has latched on to the
machinery of capitalist governance. But this would also be true of other forms
of radical organizing. Socialist third parties still have to run in accordance
with the ruling class election codes, often with piddling results. Trotskyist
rank-and-file trade unionists, while workerist in their outlook, still must
work within established unions who submit themselves to a Byzantine and often
restrictive legal regime. Unless you're practicing guerrilla tactics in the
jungle, all socialist organizing under capitalism operates within the so-
called system.

Socialists outside DSA don’t have much to fear, because DSA electoral success
doesn’t hinder the organizing work of other socialist groups. Nothing about
these victories impede worker and tenant organizing and the growing street
resistance to deportations. The DSA won’t turn the Democrats into Bolsheviks
like conservative fear, but their success may pull the nation’s center away
from the right.

The centrist Democrats are correctly worried that their post-Clinton
neoliberalism is crumbling. But judging by their current hysteria at DSA wins
they don’t understand that their years of standing for almost nothing other
than “we’re not Republicans” has made them weak enough for socialist
advancement at the grassroots level.
